title: Electromagnetic Induction (EMI)
subtitle: Zero-to-JEE-Advanced Visual Textbook: Magnetic Flux, Faraday's & Lenz's Laws, Induced Charge, Motional EMF (Translating & Rotating Rods), Induced Electric Field, Self & Mutual Inductance, RL Circuits & LC Oscillations
introduction:
💡 First-Time Reader Intuition: If Current Creates Magnetism, Can Magnetism Create Current?

In 1820, Oersted showed that an electric current produces a magnetic field. For the next 11 years, Michael Faraday asked the reverse question: Can a magnetic field produce an electric current?

At first, placing the strongest stationary magnet next to a wire coil produced zero current. Then in 1831, Faraday made a discovery that powers our entire modern electrical grid: a stationary magnetic field does nothing, but a CHANGING magnetic flux through a circuit induces an Electromotive Force (EMF) and drives an electric current!

Magnetic Flux ($\Phi_B$) & Its Units:
  • Definition: The number of magnetic field lines passing perpendicularly through a surface area $\vec{A}$: $$\boxed{\Phi_B = \int \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{A} = B A \cos\theta}$$ (where $\theta$ is the angle between $\vec{B}$ and the area normal vector $\hat{n}$!).
  • SI Unit: $1\text{ Weber (Wb)} = 1\text{ T}\cdot\text{m}^2 = 1\text{ V}\cdot\text{s} = 1\text{ J/A}$.
  • CGS Unit: $1\text{ Maxwell (Mx)}$, where $\boxed{1\text{ Weber} = 10^8\text{ Maxwell}}$.

topics.title: Faraday's Law of EMI, Lenz's Law (Conservation of Energy) & Total Induced Charge Flow
topics.theoryHtml:
1.1 Faraday's Law & Lenz's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
Faraday's Law:
The magnitude of the induced EMF in any closed loop is directly proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linked with the loop. For a coil of $N$ turns:
$$\boxed{\mathcal{E} = -N\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt} = -\frac{d}{dt}(N B A \cos\theta)} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{Average EMF:} \quad |\mathcal{E}_{\text{avg}}| = N\left|\frac{\Delta\Phi_B}{\Delta t}\right|$$
Lenz's Law (The Physical Meaning of the Minus Sign):
The polarity of the induced EMF (and direction of induced current) is always such that it OPPOSES the very cause (change in magnetic flux) that produces it.
• If inward flux ($\otimes$) is INCREASING: The loop induces a counter-clockwise current to create an outward field ($\odot$) opposing the increase.
• If inward flux ($\otimes$) is DECREASING: The loop induces a clockwise current to create an inward field ($\otimes$) trying to restore the dying flux!
Fundamental Basis: Lenz's Law is a direct consequence of the Law of Conservation of Energy (mechanical work done against opposing magnetic force converts into Joule electrical heat $I^2 Rt$).
1.2 Induced Current ($I$), Induced Charge ($\Delta q$) & Heat Dissipated

If a closed coil of total resistance $R$ (and $N$ turns) experiences a flux change from $\Phi_i$ to $\Phi_f$:

$$\text{1. Instantaneous Induced Current:} \qquad \boxed{I = \frac{|\mathcal{E}|}{R} = \frac{N}{R}\left|\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}\right|}$$
$$\text{2. Total Induced Charge Flown } (\Delta q = \int I\,dt): \qquad \boxed{\Delta q = \frac{N |\Delta\Phi_B|}{R} = \frac{N |\Phi_f - \Phi_i|}{R}}$$

Crucial JEE Rule: While induced EMF $\mathcal{E}$ and induced current $I$ depend on how fast the flux changes ($\Delta t$), the total induced charge $\Delta q = \frac{N|\Delta\Phi_B|}{R}$ depends ONLY on the net change in flux and resistance $R$—it is 100% INDEPENDENT of the time taken!
topics.derivationHtml:
Proof that Induced Charge Δq = N|ΔΦ| / R Is Independent of Time, While Heat Depends on Speed

1. Total Charge $\Delta q$: Integrating $I(t) = \frac{dq}{dt} = \frac{N}{R}\left|\frac{d\Phi}{dt}\right|$ with respect to time $t$ cancels $dt$ completely:

$$\Delta q = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} I\,dt = \int_{\Phi_i}^{\Phi_f} \frac{N}{R}|d\Phi| = \boxed{\frac{N|\Phi_f - \Phi_i|}{R}}$$

2. Total Heat Dissipated $H$: Notice that $H = \int I^2 R\,dt = \frac{1}{R}\int \mathcal{E}^2\,dt \neq \frac{(\Delta q)^2 R}{1}$! Pulling a coil out of a magnetic field twice as fast ($\Delta t \to \Delta t/2$) doubles $\mathcal{E}$ and doubles $I$, so total heat dissipated $H = I^2 R \Delta t$ DOUBLES, even though the total charge $\Delta q$ remains identical!

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Falling Bar Magnet Through a Horizontal Metal Ring):
    • If the ring is closed (complete): As the magnet approaches from above, the upper face of the ring opposes it (repulsion), and after the magnet passes through, the lower face attracts it upward. In both stages, magnetic force opposes motion, so acceleration is ALWAYS less than gravity ($a < g$)!
    • If the ring has a cut / open gap: Induced EMF still exists across the gap, but induced current is zero ($I = 0$), so no opposing magnetic force acts and the magnet falls with $a = g$!
  • Trap 2 (Flipping a Coil by $180^\circ$): When a coil initially perpendicular to $\vec{B}$ ($\theta_1 = 0^\circ, \Phi_i = +BA$) is flipped through $180^\circ$ ($\theta_2 = 180^\circ, \Phi_f = -BA$), the magnitude of flux change is $|\Delta\Phi| = |-BA - BA| = \mathbf{2BA}$ (NOT zero!), so $\Delta q = \frac{2NBA}{R}$!

topics.title: Motional EMF: Translating Conducting Rod, Rail-Gun Terminal Velocity, Effective Length & Rotating Rod/Disk in Magnetic Field

prerequisites.label: Magnetic Lorentz Force F = q(v × B)

topics.theoryHtml:
2.1 Motional EMF in a Translating Conductor ($\mathcal{E} = (\vec{v}\times\vec{B})\cdot\vec{\ell}_{\text{eff}}$)
Lorentz Force Origin of Motional EMF:
When a conducting rod of length $\ell$ moves with velocity $\vec{v}$ through a magnetic field $\vec{B}$, free electrons inside the rod experience magnetic force $\vec{F}_m = -e(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})$ and pile up at one end until the electrostatic field $E = \mathcal{E}/\ell$ balances $vB$. Thus the rod behaves like a Battery whose POSITIVE terminal is in the direction of $(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})$!
$$\text{General Scalar Triple Product Form:} \qquad \boxed{\mathcal{E} = \int (\vec{v} \times \vec{B})\cdot d\vec{\ell} = (\vec{v} \times \vec{B})\cdot \vec{L}_{\text{eff}}}$$
$$\text{When } \vec{v} \perp \vec{B} \perp \vec{\ell}: \qquad \boxed{\mathcal{E} = B v \ell}$$

Crucial JEE Rule: If ANY two of the three vectors $(\vec{v}, \vec{B}, \vec{L}_{\text{eff}})$ are parallel to each other, the motional EMF is strictly ZERO ($\mathcal{E} = 0$)! For any curved wire moving with uniform translational velocity $\vec{v}$ in uniform $\vec{B}$, replace the curved wire with the straight vector $\vec{L}_{\text{eff}} = \vec{AB}$ joining its endpoints.

2.2 Conducting Rod Sliding on Parallel Rails (Rail-Gun Mechanics)

Suppose a rod of mass $m$ and length $\ell$ slides with speed $v$ on frictionless conducting rails connected to a resistor $R$ in a perpendicular field $B$:

$$\text{1. Induced Current:} \quad \boxed{I = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{R} = \frac{B v \ell}{R}} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{2. Retarding Magnetic Force:} \quad \boxed{F_m = I \ell B = \frac{B^2 \ell^2 v}{R}}$$
$$\text{3. Mechanical Power = Electrical Thermal Power:} \qquad \boxed{P = F_m v = I^2 R = \frac{B^2 \ell^2 v^2}{R}}$$
  • Case A (Pulled by Constant External Force $F_{\text{ext}}$ or Falling Vertically Under Gravity $mg$):
    As speed $v$ increases, opposing magnetic drag $\frac{B^2\ell^2 v}{R}$ grows until it balances $F_{\text{ext}}$ (or $mg\sin\theta$), reaching Terminal Velocity:
    $$\boxed{v_T = \frac{F_{\text{ext}} R}{B^2 \ell^2}} \qquad \left(\text{On vertical/inclined rails under gravity: } \boxed{v_T = \frac{m g R \sin\theta}{B^2 \ell^2}}\right)$$
  • Case B (Given Initial Speed $v_0$ with No External Force):
    Since $m\frac{dv}{dt} = -\frac{B^2\ell^2}{R}v = -m\frac{dv}{dx}v$, speed decays exponentially $v(t) = v_0 e^{-t/\tau}$, and the total stopping distance before coming to rest is $\boxed{x_{\max} = \frac{m v_0 R}{B^2 \ell^2}}$.
2.3 Motional EMF in a Rotating Conducting Rod, Wheel & Faraday Disk

When a conducting rod of length $L$ rotates with angular speed $\omega$ ($f$ rev/s) about one end $O$ in a perpendicular magnetic field $B$, an element $dr$ at distance $r$ from the pivot moves at speed $v = \omega r$, generating $d\mathcal{E} = B(\omega r)dr$:

$$\boxed{\mathcal{E} = \int_0^L B\omega r\,dr = \frac{1}{2} B \omega L^2 = \pi B f L^2 = B A_{\text{circle}} f}$$
  • General Rotating Segment from $r = r_1$ to $r = r_2$: $\boxed{\mathcal{E} = \frac{1}{2}B\omega\left|r_2^2 - r_1^2\right|}$.
  • Rod Rotating About Its Own Midpoint (Center $C$): Both ends $A$ and $B$ are at distance $L/2$ from $C$, so $V_A - V_C = V_B - V_C = \frac{1}{2}B\omega(L/2)^2 = \frac{1}{8}B\omega L^2$, which means $\boxed{V_A - V_B = 0}$ between the two ends!
  • Bicycle Wheel with $N$ Metallic Spokes OR Solid Conducting Disk of Radius $R$:
    All $N$ spokes are connected in PARALLEL between the central axle and the outer rim! Therefore, the EMF between axle and rim is STILL $\boxed{\mathcal{E} = \frac{1}{2}B\omega R^2}$ (completely independent of the number of spokes $N$!).
topics.derivationHtml:
Classic JEE Advanced Model: Rod Sliding on Frictionless Rails Connected to an Uncharged Capacitor C (Constant Acceleration!)

Suppose a rod of mass $m$ and length $\ell$ is pulled by a constant horizontal force $F$ on smooth rails connected to an uncharged capacitor $C$ (instead of a resistor $R$) in perpendicular field $B$. Does the rod reach a terminal velocity?

Step 1: At any instant, voltage across the capacitor equals motional EMF: $V_C = \mathcal{E} = B\ell v$, so charge is $q = C\mathcal{E} = C B \ell v$.

Step 2: Differentiate $q(t)$ to find the charging current: $\boxed{I = \frac{dq}{dt} = C B \ell \frac{dv}{dt} = C B \ell a}$!

Step 3: Apply Newton's Second Law ($F - I\ell B = ma$):

$$F - (C B \ell a)\ell B = ma \implies \boxed{a = \frac{F}{m + C B^2 \ell^2} = \text{CONSTANT!}}$$

Amazing Result: With a capacitor, the rod NEVER reaches a terminal velocity—it accelerates uniformly forever with effective mass $m_{\text{eff}} = m + CB^2\ell^2$!

• Trap (East-West vs. North-South Train/Airplane Cutting Earth's Magnetic Field):
    • A horizontal rod or airplane wings moving horizontally (East-West OR North-South) cuts ONLY the VERTICAL component of Earth's magnetic field ($B_V = B_e\sin\delta$): $\boxed{\mathcal{E} = B_V v L}$! (Thus at the Magnetic Equator where $B_V = 0$, a horizontally flying airplane develops ZERO EMF across its wingtips!).
    • A vertical rod or flagpole moving East-West cuts the horizontal component $B_H$ ($\mathcal{E} = B_H v L$).
    • A rod falling vertically along North-South cuts $B_H$ ($\mathcal{E} = B_H v L$), whereas a rod held North-South and falling vertically cuts ZERO flux ($\vec{\ell} \parallel \vec{B}_H$ and $\vec{v} \parallel \vec{B}_V \implies \mathbf{\mathcal{E} = 0}$)!

topics.title: Induced (Non-Conservative) Electric Field Due to Time-Varying Magnetic Field (dB/dt), Betatron Spin-Up & AC Generator
topics.theoryHtml:
3.1 Induced Electric Field ($\oint \vec{E}_{\text{ind}}\cdot d\vec{\ell} = -\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}$)
Electrostatic Field vs. Induced Electric Field:
Even in empty space with no conducting wire present, a time-varying magnetic field ($\frac{d\vec{B}}{dt} \neq 0$) creates a circulating Induced Electric Field $\vec{E}_{\text{ind}}$:
• Electrostatic Field (from static charges): Conservative ($\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{\ell} = 0$), open field lines starting on $+q$ and ending on $-q$.
• Induced Electric Field (from $d\vec{B}/dt$): NON-CONSERVATIVE ($\oint \vec{E}_{\text{ind}}\cdot d\vec{\ell} = -\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt} \neq 0$), forms closed circular loops with no start or end! Potential $V$ is NOT defined for an induced electric field!

Cylindrical Region of Radius $R$ with Uniform Time-Varying Field $B(t)$:

$$\text{1. Inside Region } (r \le R): \quad E(2\pi r) = (\pi r^2)\left|\frac{dB}{dt}\right| \implies \boxed{E_{\text{in}}(r) = \frac{r}{2}\left|\frac{dB}{dt}\right|} \quad (E \propto r)$$
$$\text{2. Outside Region } (r > R): \quad E(2\pi r) = (\pi R^2)\left|\frac{dB}{dt}\right| \implies \boxed{E_{\text{out}}(r) = \frac{R^2}{2r}\left|\frac{dB}{dt}\right|} \quad \left(E \propto \frac{1}{r}\right)$$
3.2 AC Generator (Rotating Coil in Uniform Magnetic Field $\vec{B}$)

When a coil of $N$ turns and area $A$ rotates with constant angular speed $\omega$ in a uniform magnetic field $B$, the flux linked at time $t$ is $\Phi_B(t) = N B A \cos(\omega t)$. Differentiating gives the sinusoidal alternating EMF:

$$\boxed{\mathcal{E}(t) = -\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt} = N B A \omega \sin(\omega t) = \mathcal{E}_0 \sin(\omega t)} \qquad \left(\text{Peak EMF } \boxed{\mathcal{E}_0 = N B A \omega}\right)$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Angular Acceleration of a Charged Non-Conducting Ring in a Time-Varying Magnetic Field

A thin insulating ring of mass $m$, radius $r \le R$, and uniform total charge $Q$ is placed concentrically inside a cylindrical magnetic field $B(t)$. When $B(t)$ changes at rate $\frac{dB}{dt}$, the tangential induced electric field $E = \frac{r}{2}\left|\frac{dB}{dt}\right|$ exerts a net torque on the ring:

$$\tau = (Q E) r = Q\left(\frac{r}{2}\left|\frac{dB}{dt}\right|\right)r = \frac{1}{2}Q r^2 \left|\frac{dB}{dt}\right|$$

Dividing by the ring's moment of inertia $I = m r^2$ gives the angular acceleration:

$$\boxed{\alpha = \frac{\tau}{I} = \frac{Q}{2m}\left|\frac{dB}{dt}\right| \implies \omega(t) = \frac{Q}{2m}|\Delta B|}$$

topics.title: Self-Inductance (L), Mutual Inductance (M), Series/Parallel Inductors, Magnetic Energy, RL Transients & LC Oscillations
topics.theoryHtml:
4.1 Self-Inductance ($L$), Mutual Inductance ($M$) & Magnetic Field Energy Density
Inductance = Electrical Inertia!
An inductor ($L$, SI unit: $1\text{ Henry (H)} = 1\text{ Wb/A} = 1\,\Omega\cdot\text{s}$) opposes any change in the current flowing through it by developing a back-EMF $\mathcal{E}_L = -L\frac{dI}{dt}$. Because magnetic flux cannot change instantaneously without infinite voltage, current through an inductor is ALWAYS continuous ($I(t^+) = I(t^-)$)!
$$\text{1. Self-Inductance:} \quad \boxed{N\Phi_B = L I \implies \mathcal{E}_L = -L\frac{dI}{dt}} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{2. Mutual Inductance:} \quad \boxed{N_2 \Phi_{21} = M I_1 \implies \mathcal{E}_2 = -M\frac{dI_1}{dt}}$$
Inductor / Coaxial SystemInductance Formula
1. Long Solenoid (Radius $r$, length $\ell \gg r$, $n = N/\ell$, relative permeability $\mu_r$)$$\boxed{L = \mu_0 \mu_r n^2 A \ell = \frac{\mu_0 \mu_r N^2 (\pi r^2)}{\ell}}$$
2. Two Coaxial Solenoids (Radii $r_1 < r_2$, length $\ell$, turns $N_1, N_2$)$$\boxed{M_{12} = M_{21} = \frac{\mu_0 N_1 N_2 (\pi r_1^2)}{\ell}} \quad (\text{Uses INNER smaller area } \pi r_1^2!)$$
3. Two Small Concentric Coplanar Loops (Radii $r \ll R$)$$\boxed{M = \frac{\mu_0 \pi r^2}{2 R}}$$
4. Coupled Inductors (Coefficient of coupling $k \in [0,1]$, $M = k\sqrt{L_1 L_2}$)• Series Aiding / Opposing: $\boxed{L_{\text{eq}} = L_1 + L_2 \pm 2M}$
• Parallel (Unlinked $M=0$): $\boxed{\frac{1}{L_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{L_1} + \frac{1}{L_2}}$
$$\textbf{Magnetic Energy Stored in Inductor:} \quad \boxed{U_B = \frac{1}{2}L I^2} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \textbf{Magnetic Energy Density:} \quad \boxed{u_B = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}}$$
4.2 RL Transient Circuits ($\tau = \frac{L}{R}$) & Undamped LC Oscillations
How an Inductor Behaves at $t = 0^+$ vs. $t \to \infty$ (Exact Opposite of a Capacitor!):
• At $t = 0^+$ (Just After Closing Switch, Initial $I = 0$): Inductor opposes the sudden current jump and acts like an OPEN CIRCUIT (BROKEN WIRE, $I_L(0^+) = 0$)!
• At $t \to \infty$ (Steady State, Constant Current $dI/dt = 0$): Back-EMF $\mathcal{E}_L = -L(0) = 0$, so an ideal inductor acts like a CLOSED WIRE (SHORT CIRCUIT, Zero Resistance!).
$$\textbf{1. RL Current Growth } (I_0 = \mathcal{E}/R, \; \tau = L/R): \quad \boxed{I(t) = I_0\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right)} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \textbf{2. RL Current Decay:} \quad \boxed{I(t) = I_0 e^{-t/\tau}}$$
$$\textbf{3. LC Electromagnetic Oscillations } \left(\frac{d^2q}{dt^2} + \frac{1}{LC}q = 0\right): \qquad \boxed{\omega = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} \implies T = 2\pi\sqrt{LC}, \qquad f = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}}$$

In an LC circuit, energy sloshes back and forth harmonically between the capacitor's electric field and the inductor's magnetic field: $\boxed{E_{\text{total}} = \frac{q^2}{2C} + \frac{1}{2}L I^2 = \frac{Q_{\max}^2}{2C} = \frac{1}{2}L I_{\max}^2}$ (where $I_{\max} = \omega Q_{\max} = \frac{Q_{\max}}{\sqrt{LC}}$).
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation of Solenoid Self-Inductance L = μ₀ n² A ℓ and Magnetic Energy Density u_B = B² / (2μ₀)

1. Self-Inductance of Solenoid: Inside a solenoid of length $\ell$, area $A$, and $N = n\ell$ turns carrying current $I$, the magnetic field is $B = \mu_0 n I$. Total flux linkage through all $N$ turns is:

$$N\Phi_B = (n\ell)(B A) = (n\ell)(\mu_0 n I)A = (\mu_0 n^2 A \ell)I \implies \boxed{L = \mu_0 n^2 A \ell}$$

2. Magnetic Energy Density: Substitute $L = \mu_0 n^2 A \ell$ and $I = \frac{B}{\mu_0 n}$ into $U = \frac{1}{2}LI^2$, and divide by volume $V = A\ell$:

$$u_B = \frac{\frac{1}{2}(\mu_0 n^2 A \ell)\left(\frac{B}{\mu_0 n}\right)^2}{A\ell} = \boxed{\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}}$$

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (KVL Potential Drop Across an Inductor When Current Is Decreasing!): When you move from $A$ to $B$ in the direction of current $I$, the KVL equation is ALWAYS $V_A - L\frac{dI}{dt} = V_B$. If the current is DECREASING at rate $5\text{ A/s}$, you MUST substitute $\mathbf{\frac{dI}{dt} = -5\text{ A/s}}$, which makes $V_B > V_A$ (the inductor acts as a battery trying to keep the dying current alive)!

conclusion: You have mastered Chapter 20: Electromagnetic Induction! Next, in Chapter 21, we apply inductors and capacitors to sinusoidal AC circuits, phasor impedance triangles, transformers, and Maxwell's Electromagnetic Waves.
summary:
• Faraday & Lenz: $\mathcal{E} = -N\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt}$; Induced charge $\Delta q = \frac{N|\Delta\Phi_B|}{R}$ (independent of time).
  • Motional EMF: Translating rod $\mathcal{E} = Bv\ell$, terminal speed $v_T = \frac{FR}{B^2\ell^2}$; Rotating rod/wheel $\mathcal{E} = \frac{1}{2}B\omega L^2$.
  • Induced E-Field: Inside cylinder $E = \frac{r}{2}|dB/dt|$; outside $E = \frac{R^2}{2r}|dB/dt|$.
  • Inductance & RL/LC: Solenoid $L = \mu_0 n^2 A\ell$, $U = \frac{1}{2}LI^2$, $u_B = \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}$; RL $\tau = L/R$; LC $\omega = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$.
formulaSheetHtml:
ConceptMaster FormulaKey Notes
Faraday's Law & Charge$\mathcal{E} = -N\dfrac{d\Phi_B}{dt}, \qquad \Delta q = \dfrac{N|\Delta\Phi_B|}{R}$$\Delta q$ depends only on net flux change.
Motional EMF (Trans & Rot)$\mathcal{E}_{\text{trans}} = (\vec{v}\times\vec{B})\cdot\vec{\ell}, \qquad \mathcal{E}_{\text{rot}} = \dfrac{1}{2}B\omega L^2$Spoked wheel has all spokes in parallel.
Induced Electric Field$E_{\text{in}} = \dfrac{r}{2}\left|\dfrac{dB}{dt}\right|, \qquad E_{\text{out}} = \dfrac{R^2}{2r}\left|\dfrac{dB}{dt}\right|$Non-conservative closed circular lines.
Solenoid & Coaxial $L, M$$L = \mu_0 n^2 A\ell, \qquad M = \dfrac{\mu_0 N_1 N_2 (\pi r_1^2)}{\ell}$$M$ always uses inner smaller radius $r_1$.
RL & LC Circuits$\tau_{RL} = \dfrac{L}{R}, \qquad \omega_{LC} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$At $t=0^+$ inductor is open; at $t\to\infty$ short.

questions.prompt: A circular coil of $N = 50$ turns, area $A = 0.02\text{ m}^2$, and total resistance $R = 10\,\Omega$ is placed perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of $B = 0.4\text{ T}$. If the coil is quickly flipped through $180^\circ$ in $0.1\text{ s}$, what is the total induced charge $\Delta q$ that flows through the coil?
questions.explanation: Flipping by $180^\circ$ changes flux from $+BA$ to $-BA$, so $|\Delta\Phi_B| = 2BA = 2(0.4)(0.02) = 0.016\text{ Wb}$. Total charge $\Delta q = \frac{N|\Delta\Phi_B|}{R} = \frac{50 \times 0.016}{10} = 0.08\text{ C}$ (completely independent of the $0.1\text{ s}$ duration!).

questions.prompt: A metallic wheel with $20$ spokes, each of length $L = 0.5\text{ m}$, is rotated at an angular speed of $\omega = 120\text{ rad/s}$ in a plane perpendicular to a magnetic field of $B = 0.4\text{ T}$. What is the induced EMF between the axle and the rim of the wheel?
questions.explanation: All 20 spokes are connected in parallel between the axle and rim, so the EMF is equal to that of a single spoke: $\mathcal{E} = \frac{1}{2}B\omega L^2 = \frac{1}{2}(0.4)(120)(0.5)^2 = 24 \times 0.25 = 6\text{ V}$.

questions.prompt: In a circuit Segment $A \to B$, a current of $I = 2\text{ A}$ flows from $A$ to $B$ through a resistor $R = 3\,\Omega$, a battery of EMF $10\text{ V}$ (with positive terminal facing $A$), and an inductor $L = 4\text{ H}$. If the current $I$ is DECREASING at a rate of $5\text{ A/s}$, what is the potential difference $V_A - V_B$?
questions.explanation: Since the current is decreasing, $\frac{dI}{dt} = -5\text{ A/s}$. Applying KVL from $A$ to $B$ along the direction of current: $V_A - I R - 10 - L\frac{dI}{dt} = V_B \implies V_A - V_B = (2)(3) + 10 + 4(-5) = 6 + 10 - 20 = -4\text{ V}$.

questions.prompt: A conducting rod of length $\ell = 1\text{ m}$ and mass $m = 0.2\text{ kg}$ slides down frictionless vertical parallel conducting rails connected at the top by a resistor $R = 2\,\Omega$ in a uniform horizontal magnetic field $B = 1\text{ T}$ perpendicular to the rails. What is the terminal velocity $v_T$ of the rod? ($g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.explanation: At terminal velocity, downward gravity $mg$ equals upward magnetic drag $\frac{B^2\ell^2 v_T}{R} \implies v_T = \frac{mgR}{B^2\ell^2} = \frac{(0.2)(10)(2)}{1^2 \times 1^2} = 4\text{ m/s}$.

questions.prompt: A capacitor of capacitance $C = 100\,\mu\text{F}$ is charged to $V_0 = 50\text{ V}$ and then connected across an ideal inductor of inductance $L = 10\text{ mH}$. What is the maximum current $I_{\max}$ that flows during the resulting LC oscillations?
questions.explanation: By energy conservation in an ideal LC circuit, $\frac{1}{2}L I_{\max}^2 = \frac{1}{2}C V_0^2 \implies I_{\max} = V_0 \sqrt{\frac{C}{L}} = 50 \sqrt{\frac{10^{-4}\text{ F}}{10^{-2}\text{ H}}} = 50 \times 0.1 = 5\text{ A}$.

questions.prompt: A small square loop of side $a$ and resistance $R$ is placed at the center of a much larger coplanar circular loop of radius $b \gg a$. If the current in the large circular loop varies with time as $I(t) = I_0 t$, what is the magnitude of the induced current in the small square loop?
questions.explanation: Because $a \ll b$, the magnetic field produced by the large circular loop at its center is uniform over the small square and equal to $B_1 = \frac{\mu_0 I_1}{2b}$. Flux through the small square is $\Phi_2 = B_1 a^2 = \left(\frac{\mu_0 a^2}{2b}\right)I_1 \implies M = \frac{\mu_0 a^2}{2b}$. Induced EMF is $\mathcal{E}_2 = M\frac{dI_1}{dt} = \frac{\mu_0 I_0 a^2}{2b}$, so induced current is $I_2 = \frac{\mathcal{E}_2}{R} = \frac{\mu_0 I_0 a^2}{2bR}$.
